properties.description: Brigsby Bear (2017), directed by Dave McCary and starring Kyle Mooney, Jorge Lendeborg Jr., and Matt Walsh, is a comedy-drama about a man raised in an underground bunker who, upon being freed, decides to make a movie based on the only TV show he ever knew. The film blends indie, coming-of-age sensibilities with warm humor and emotional depth as it examines identity, parental deception, and the healing power of creativity. Produced with involvement from members of The Lonely Island, the movie balances quirky, handmade visuals with heartfelt performances to create a bittersweet, uplifting experience.
properties.plot_summary: A sheltered man raised underground on a single, homemade children’s TV show is abruptly freed and confronted with the truth about his upbringing. Struggling to adapt to the outside world, he becomes determined to honor the only narrative he has ever known by making a film based on that show. His project draws in new friends and reluctant relatives, forcing him to reckon with betrayal, identity, and the possibility of belonging. Through collaborative creativity he seeks to transform isolation and trauma into connection and purpose.

properties.description: The Big Short (2015), directed by Adam McKay and adapted from Michael Lewis's book, follows several investors who foresee and bet against the U.S. housing bubble. Starring Christian Bale, Steve Carell, and Ryan Gosling, the film blends biography, dark comedy, and historical drama to reveal widespread fraud and systemic failure in financial institutions. Its sharp, satirical tone and inventive explanatory devices turn dense economic subjects into an emotionally charged critique of greed and accountability.
properties.plot_summary: In the mid‑2000s a handful of contrarian investors recognize that the U.S. mortgage market is built on unstable subprime loans and complex securities. Betting against that market, they dig into banks, rating agencies, and the instruments that hide risk. Their research exposes widespread fraud, negligence, and systemic failure as the housing bubble unravels. The film balances sharp satire and explanatory detours to make dense financial mechanics emotionally and morally resonant.

properties.description: Inherent Vice (2014), directed by Paul Thomas Anderson and starring Joaquin Phoenix, Josh Brolin, Owen Wilson and Katherine Waterston, is a psychedelic neo-noir comedy-crime drama set in early-1970s Los Angeles. An affable, pot-smoking private investigator becomes entangled in a labyrinthine missing-person case that unravels into conspiracies, land deals and corrupt authority figures. Adapted from Thomas Pynchon's novel, the film blends stoner humor, melancholic nostalgia and surreal visual flourishes to explore paranoia, disillusionment and the twilight of the countercultural moment.
properties.plot_summary: In 1970 Los Angeles, pot-smoking private eye Larry “Doc” Sportello is visited by his former lover, who asks for help rescuing her real-estate magnate boyfriend from a bizarre scheme. When the mogul vanishes and bodies begin to turn up, Doc follows a convoluted trail through land grabs, black radicals, hypnotic parties and corrupt authority figures. The investigation unspools as a hallucinatory, humor-tinged noir where loyalties blur, conspiracies proliferate, and the countercultural optimism of the era curdles into paranoia. The film mixes stoned comedy with melancholic nostalgia as Doc struggles to make sense of a world that is already changing around him.
